wine.name: Barbár
wine.grapes: Cabernet Franc in the lead, with Merlot, Tannat and Kékfrankos; the shares move with the vintage.
wine.sites: Grown from the family's first vineyard, planted in 2002 on the crest of the Porkoláb valley on Szekszárd's loess, by the house's account; the Cabernet Franc of that ridge is the blend's backbone.
wine.making: Made only in vintages the family judges fully ripe and healthy. Each variety is raised apart for about a year in barrels of 300, 500 and 1,000 litres, mostly second and third fill with a small share of new oak, as the merchant's sheet for the 2020 vintage gives it; the blend then rests for over a year in bottle before release.
wine.glass: Black cherry, blackcurrant and plum with cedar, tobacco leaf and black pepper; full and dense, Tannat giving firm, grippy tannin and Kékfrankos a lift of fresh acidity.
wine.ageing: Firm in its youth and built by the house to age, it wants five years or more after release and a ripe vintage keeps for well over a decade.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour or two; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The house's own name for its flagship blend, taken by its account from Bartók's piano piece Allegro barbaro.

records.table: Cabernet Franc leads Heimann's Barbár, with Merlot, Tannat and Kékfrankos beside it, a Szekszárd red the family makes only in strong years. Dense and firm, black cherry and pepper over grippy tannin, it needs air and a plate of red meat.
records.story: The Heimann family dates its life in Szekszárd to 1758, when its name first appears there in a marriage record, and counts itself among the town's families of German descent who farmed the loess hills. The estate as a guest meets it is far younger. In 2002 the family planted its first vineyard of its own on the crest of the Porkoláb valley, and Barbár grew from it: a blend led by Cabernet Franc from that ridge, with Merlot, Tannat for grip and Kékfrankos for freshness, made only in vintages the family judges ripe and sound. It stands among Szekszárd's own named blends, a bigger and more intense cousin of the district's Bikavér. From 2005 the family planted a selection of Kadarka clones gathered from the district's old vineyards, the work that made the house a voice for the native grape, and the next generation carried it into single vineyard Kadarka and Kékfrankos under the Heimann & Fiai label, Heimann and Sons. The name, by the house's account, comes from Allegro barbaro, the piano piece by Béla Bartók (1881 to 1945), and in the 2020s Barbarossa joined Barbár as its second wine, from the same four grapes. What Barbár teaches is how Szekszárd's loess carries Bordeaux varieties once Tannat and Kékfrankos sharpen the frame.

wine.name: Regnum
wine.grapes: Merlot and Cabernet Franc in the lead, with Cabernet Sauvignon and, from later vintages, Kékfrankos and Syrah; the mix moves with the year.
wine.sites: The family's vineyards on Szekszárd's loess hills west of the Danube, where the warm southern climate ripens Bordeaux varieties fully.
wine.making: Raised in oak barrels before it is bottled, in the Bordeaux manner the name promises. The house's own sheet for the vessels, the origin of the oak and the months was not reached, and one merchant's figures alone are not enough to teach, so the record gives none.

wine.ageing: Soft enough to open a few years after release, it turns more savoury across five to ten years in a cool cellar.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour; a Bordeaux glass.

records.table: Takler's Regnum, Latin for kingdom, is a Szekszárd blend in the Bordeaux manner: Merlot and Cabernet Franc in the lead, Cabernet Sauvignon beside them. Ripe plum and cassis over clove and soft, fine tannin show the district's warmth; give it an hour in a decanter.
records.story: The Takler family farmed vines in Szekszárd long before the communist years, when the district's private vineyards, cellars and wine passed to the state. The modern estate began in 1996, when the founder, born into that family in those years, set up a winery of his own, and with his two sons he built it into one of the district's large houses, bottling its own wines. Regnum, Latin for kingdom, is the blend that set its course: Merlot and Cabernet Franc in the lead with Cabernet Sauvignon, raised in oak in the Bordeaux manner. In 2004 the founder was named Hungary's Winemaker of the Year. The family marked the estate's twentieth anniversary in 2016, and by then the range reached back to the district's own grapes as well: Kékfrankos from single hills, a Szekszárdi Bikavér named Örökség, heritage, and the old Kadarka, while Kékfrankos and Syrah have joined Regnum's blend in later vintages. Regnum stands for Szekszárd's warm, round take on Bordeaux varieties, the style that made the district's modern name abroad, beside the native reds that have come back since.

wine.name: Nagyapám Kadarka
wine.grapes: Kadarka, Szekszárd's old native red grape, alone.
wine.sites: The selected fruit of the estate's old Kadarka vines in the family's valleys of Szekszárd, among them Bodzás, Görögszó, the Porkoláb valley and the Palánki hill, with vines from its own clone selection trials.
wine.making: Made to keep Kadarka's pale colour and perfume. The 2024 was raised in stainless steel alone, with no barrel at all, while the 2016, by one importer's account, was raised in steel and oak together; the vessels move with the year.
wine.glass: Ripe cherry, raspberry and plum with black pepper and a hint of rose; light in colour and body, with soft tannin and a fresh, juicy line of acidity.
wine.ageing: Charming on release, it keeps its fruit for three to five years, the span the house gives one vintage, and gains a gentle savoury edge.
wine.serve: 13 to 15 degrees Celsius, cool like a light red; no need to decant; a Burgundy glass.

records.table: From the family's old vines and its own clone trials comes Nagyapám, My Grandfather, Eszterbauer's Szekszárd Kadarka. Pale and perfumed, all cherry, raspberry and pepper over soft tannin, it answers a guest who wonders how the district's native red tastes.
records.story: Szekszárd's red wine owes much to settlers. Serbian refugees from the Ottoman advance are thought to have brought Kadarka and the southern Slav way with red wine, and after the Ottoman wars Hungarian and German settlers replanted the hills. The Eszterbauers appear in the town's vineyard records from 1746, and the family counts ten generations on its land. Kadarka became the district's flagship grape in the nineteenth century, before phylloxera ruined the vineyards late in that century. Some old plantings survive: one of the family's Kadarka plots was set out in 1912 as bush vines. Over the twentieth century Kadarka lost ground to Kékfrankos and the Bordeaux varieties, and its return has rested on growers who went back to such old vines. The Eszterbauers did so through clone selection trials on their own old plantings, and Nagyapám is the fruit of that work: the selected grapes of the old vines, made to keep the grape's pale colour and perfume. The name means my grandfather, a tribute to a forebear who owned vineyards in the town. Light, peppery and fresh, Nagyapám pours the old grape of Szekszárd on its own.

wine.name: Valles Szekszárdi Bikavér Prémium
wine.classification: Prémium, the upper of the two tiers of Szekszárdi Bikavér
wine.grapes: Kékfrankos, about half, with Merlot, Cabernet Franc and a little Kadarka; the mix moves with the year.
wine.sites: A blend across the family's valley vineyards, as its Latin name, valleys, suggests; the house's named sites include Hidaspetre and Bakta, on Szekszárd's loess.

Every Szekszárdi Bikavér, regular or Prémium, must spend at least a year in oak.
wine.glass: Sour cherry, ripe plum and blackberry with black pepper, clove and a savoury, smoky edge; medium bodied and elegant, the fresh acidity of Kékfrankos carrying fine, ripe tannin.
wine.ageing: Open a few years after release; a ripe vintage keeps for eight to ten years, turning more savoury as it goes.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour; a Bordeaux glass.

records.table: Valles, the Vida family's Prémium Szekszárdi Bikavér, is about half Kékfrankos, with Merlot, Cabernet Franc and a touch of Kadarka, raised mostly in large oak casks. Sour cherry and pepper over fine tannin, it is the district's Bull's Blood in the upper of its two tiers.
records.story: Two towns lay claim to Bikavér, bull's blood. A drinking song of 1846 by a poet of Szekszárd praised the dark wine of its hills, but under communism Eger alone used the name, and Szekszárd won it back only at the end of the 1980s. The Vida family's estate began in the years after that change and grew into a family house of the district working Kadarka, Kékfrankos and Bikavér. In 2011 its founder was named Hungary's Winemaker of the Year. From the 2020 harvest a daughter, back from making wine in New Zealand, joined the cellar, and the family has since described the house as a team of generations rather than one maker. Its single vineyard Kékfrankos from Hidaspetre shows one valley; Valles, Latin for valleys, gathers several into the Prémium tier of Szekszárdi Bikavér, the upper of the district's two, whose wines, like the regular tier's, spend at least a year in oak. Valles puts Szekszárd's Bikavér plainly: Kékfrankos at its heart, with Merlot, Cabernet Franc and the district's own Kadarka.

records.story: The Vesztergombi family traces its vines in Szekszárd to the early eighteenth century, by its own account, and the house names a Vesztergombi as the town's first vineyard judge, the office that brought the hillside's growers into order and kept their wine on record. Its business is a recent one. In 1991, as land taken under communism was handed back, the family recovered vines and a cellar on Kadarka Street and founded the business, and in 1993 its founder was named Hungary's Winemaker of the Year, early in the district's revival. The house grew around Bikavér and Kadarka, with its cellar later on Borkút Street. Its St. László Bikavér, named for the town's patron saint and raised for two years in new oak barrels of 300 and 500 litres, won the Bikavér category of the Hungarian Parliament's wine selection with its 2019 vintage. Beside the blends, the family bottles Kékfrankos from single valleys, and the Porkoláb valley, a site several Szekszárd houses name on their labels, gives the one taught here: Kékfrankos alone, two years in oak. Firm, peppery and fresh, it is Kékfrankos read through one valley by a family that has worked these hills for generations.

others.note: The house's Szekszárdi Bikavér, named for the town's patron saint; the 2019 spent two years in new 300 and 500 litre oak and six months in bottle.

others.name: Kadarka
others.note: The house's Kadarka bottled alone, from the district's historic red grape.

traps: Porkolábvölgy names a valley, not a producer: several Szekszárd houses, among them Heimann and Eszterbauer, farm vines in the Porkoláb valley.
The Porkolábvölgy wine is Kékfrankos alone; the house's blend is its St. László Bikavér.

Six months in new French barriques

questions.exp: The house's sheet for 2019 gives about 24 months in barrels of 300 to 500 litres; six months in barriques is far shorter than its long élevage.

questions.q: In which year did the Vesztergombi family found its modern Szekszárd house, as vines and a cellar came back to it?
questions.exp: The business was founded in 1991, after land was handed back; 1993 is the year its founder was named Hungary's Winemaker of the Year.

report: The plan asked whether Bikavér is the wine the house leads with: St. László Bikavér is the house's Parliament wine and the plan's why calls the house known for Bikavér and Kadarka, so a swap of the flagship to St. László Bikavér may be fairer; the Porkoláb Kékfrankos is kept under the plan's key and taught as the house's single vineyard Kékfrankos.

Founded 1991 rests on the house's page, the Wines of Hungary listing and Hungarianwines.eu; the family's roots are given by the house as the early 1700s in one place and the 1600s in another, so the story says the early eighteenth century by its own account.
Winemaker of the Year 1993 rests on Hungarianwines.eu and the house's page; the founder, his wife and son are living and none is named, nor the forebear who was vineyard judge, for want of dates.

The label words: Wines of Hungary prints Porkolábvölgy Kékfrankos, a merchant prints Szekszárdi Kékfrankos Porkolábvölgy; wine.name is written Porkoláb-völgy Kékfrankos so the lint finds the plan's word, and the label term keeps the printed Porkolábvölgy: the integrator may prefer the printed form.
The barrel time rests on the house's sheet for 2019 alone; the fermentation vessels are not given in any source read.
The Kadarka's two years in steel and oak rests on a Wines of Hungary listing for 2022.

changed: story: was a forebear who served as first vineyard judge and brought a formal register; the house names a György Vesztergombi as the first vineyard judge with no tie or dates, so now the house names a Vesztergombi, and the office is told as the house tells it.
story: was a new winery on Borkút Street where the reds are aged; now its cellar later on Borkút Street (hungarianwines.eu).
story, others: St. László Bikavér now named for the town's patron saint and the winner of the Parliament's Bikavér category with the 2019 (parlament.hu, Hungary Today).
others: the Kadarka's two years in steel and oak cut (one listing).
traps: Sebestyén, not found in the Porkoláb valley, gave way to Eszterbauer, whose plots there the Parliament page names.
wine.serve: was 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; now 15 to 17, the Codex's medium red, as for the group's other Kékfrankos led wine.
open: Whether Porkolábvölgy Kékfrankos is the house's flagship stays open: St. László Bikavér is its Parliament winner; the swap is refused here for the group's balance (see the review).
The label prints Porkolábvölgy; wine.name keeps the plan's Porkoláb-völgy form for the integrator to settle.
